job.style: a diary entry or letter by a student

passage: Dear Diary, today my father explained why we must be careful with money. He showed me two loan offers for a new bike. One bank uses a flat rate of 8%, while the other uses a reducing-balance rate of 8%. He warned that the flat rate is actually much more expensive because you pay interest on the full amount even as you pay it back. He also checked a credit card statement, noting that the interest-free period only applies if you pay the full bill, not just a part of it. We then calculated interest for a six-month loan. Since the formula uses time in years, we had to use 0.5 years, not 6, to get the correct amount. Finally, he explained that while a 10-year loan has a smaller monthly EMI, you end up paying much more in total interest than with a 2-year loan. I realized that borrowing is not just about the interest rate or the monthly payment; it is about the total cost over time. I must always check the fine print before agreeing to any loan or using a credit card.

items.evidence: He warned that the flat rate is actually much more expensive because you pay interest on the full amount even as you pay it back.
items.q: Two banks both offer a bike loan at 8%. How do the flat-rate and reducing-balance offers compare?
options: The flat-rate loan costs much more overall
Both cost the same, since the rates are equal
The reducing-balance loan costs much more overall
Neither has extra costs, since 8% is low
items.explain: A flat rate charges interest on the full amount even as you repay, so it costs more than reducing-balance.

wrong.why: thinks the same rate number means the same cost
reverses which loan is more expensive
thinks a low rate means no other costs

items.evidence: He also checked a credit card statement, noting that the interest-free period only applies if you pay the full bill, not just a part of it.
items.q: Meena pays only half of her credit card bill by the due date. What happens to her interest-free period?
options: She loses it and must pay interest
It still covers the whole bill
It still applies, since card rates are low
It is extended by one more month
items.explain: The interest-free period only applies if you pay the full bill, not just part of it.

wrong.why: thinks a part payment keeps the interest-free period
thinks a low rate means nothing to worry about
guesses that paying something earns extra time

items.evidence: Since the formula uses time in years, we had to use 0.5 years, not 6, to get the correct amount.
items.q: To find simple interest on a six-month loan, what value of T should go into SI = PRT/100?
options: 0.5, because T must be in years
6, because the loan lasts six months
1, because the loan length does not matter
12, because a year has twelve months
items.explain: The formula uses time in years, so six months is 0.5 years, not 6.

wrong.why: puts the number of months straight into the formula
thinks interest does not depend on time
picks a nearby number linked to months

items.evidence: Finally, he explained that while a 10-year loan has a smaller monthly EMI, you end up paying much more in total interest than with a 2-year loan.
items.q: Kabir chooses a 10-year loan over a 2-year loan because its EMI is smaller. What is the result?
options: He pays much more interest in total
He pays less in total, as EMIs are smaller
He pays the same interest, as time doesn't matter
He pays less interest, but a bigger EMI
items.explain: A 10-year loan has a smaller EMI, but you pay much more total interest than with a 2-year loan.

wrong.why: thinks smaller EMIs mean a smaller total cost
thinks interest does not depend on time
mixes up which loan has the smaller EMI
